name: Priya Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. I'll be straight with you, that's how I am.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at five, check the AI farm app for weather and soil, then feed the suckler cows and check the calves. By seven I'm usually in a tractor, either on my own fields or drilling and spraying for a neighbour. I love the contracting, being out on different farms; what wears me out is chasing late payers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the farm and your family.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lowfield is 300 hectares of wheat and oilseed rape with 120 suckler cows, and my contracting business works for twelve neighbouring farms. I took it over from my parents and built the contracting myself. My husband Kwame tests software for a bank, and we've got Ama, who's thirteen, and Kofi, who's ten, and a mortgage on the farmhouse we renovated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Now I'll read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a good tool and I'll keep using it. I use AI every day to plan sprays, book contract jobs and read soil tests, and that won't change. I'd tell the other farmers at the discussion group they're missing a trick if they don't use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means business as usual, and business is good. I run Lowfield, 300 hectares of wheat and oilseed rape plus 120 suckler cows, and a contracting business drilling and spraying for twelve neighbours. Kwame's software job pays well, and we've got savings and the land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the new GPS sprayer we've been eyeing, about 95,000, with a loan and some savings. I'd sign up two more contracting clients over the winter. Everything else stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit bored with all the hype. My worries are the usual ones, like a dry spring or a breakdown in the middle of drilling. The money side feels solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the others are missing a trick. What does AI actually do for you on a normal day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This morning it read the weather and the soil moisture and told me which fields I could spray before the rain. It booked three contracting jobs by text while I was in the tractor. The AI saves me about two hours a day, and in harvest that's two hours of sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you work with most closely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My operator, Danny, who drives the second tractor. Danny is twenty-six, brilliant on the machines, and I'm training him to run the contracting side. In this picture he gets more responsibility and a raise next year.

I'd tell the **discussion group** they're missing a trick without it.
think: I think it's **business as usual**, and business is good.
Our **land, savings** and Kwame's pay make us secure.
do: Buy the **GPS sprayer** for about 95,000 with a loan and savings.
Sign up **two more contracting clients** over the winter.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** with the hype.

steps.text: Buy the new GPS sprayer with a loan and savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly good for farmers who use it and hard on office workers. At the discussion group I'd tell people to get ahead of it. And I'd probably post something practical, like which apps actually work for booking and planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worry is Kwame, not me. Kwame tests software for a bank, and checking is one of the first things this picture takes over. My farm and contracting get better with these tools, but our second income could shrink fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move all the contracting bookings and invoices to an AI system by spring and take on four more clients. I'd start a drone crop-scouting service for neighbours, and Kwame could run the data side two days a week if his hours get cut. And we'd add 1,000 a month to savings until his job looks settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I wouldn't show it. My business gets stronger, but Kwame's job is exactly the kind that shrinks. I can see a way through, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Kwame could run the data side. Has he agreed to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet, and that's a big conversation. Kwame likes his job and his colleagues, and he's never wanted to be a farmer. But he likes numbers, and a drone scouting service is basically numbers with a view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if Kwame's pay drops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car, probably, and the holiday in Ghana to see his family would get shorter. I'd keep the kids' music lessons and the farm investments. The farm is what pays in the long run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, adapt or get left behind. I wouldn't sugar-coat it at the discussion group. I'd say the farmers who buy robots early will be fine and the ones who wait will struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my contracting business is in trouble by 2031. If every farmer can buy a robot tractor that drills and sprays on its own, nobody needs to pay me to come and do it. And Kwame's job is likely gone by 2028, so the household loses one income fast and part of the other later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell the older contracting machines in 2029 while they still have value. I'd buy the first robot tractors I can trust, probably 2030, and offer robot contracting to farmers who can't afford their own. And I'd build the savings up to two years of household costs while Kwame finds his feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. I can see what to do, but two years is short. I'd be working flat out the whole time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and the robots about three years later. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The gap is my window, really. The thinking part of farming, planning sprays and booking jobs, I already do with AI, so 2028 changes little for my work. Those three years are when I sell the old kit, buy the robots and get my customers signed up before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'adapt or get left behind'. What about farmers who can't adapt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part, and I don't have a good answer. My neighbour Ted is sixty and still uses a paper map of his fields. I'd offer him a deal to do his work with my robots, but plenty of farmers like Ted would just sell up.

I'd say **early robot buyers** will be fine and the waiters will struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so use it, and I'd say it at the discussion group. Like with the fast one, the early movers will win, but five years means more people can catch up. I'd run a session on robot tractors for the group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a comfortable runway for me. Kwame has time to retrain into something like farm data or drone mapping, and I can switch the contracting to robots step by step. I think we come out ahead, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the current kit till about 2031 and then replace it with robots one machine at a time. I'd put the drone scouting service on a proper footing, with Kwame full time by 2030. And I'd do an online course in robot fleet management, because that's the job I'll be doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I'm used to. There's change coming and I'm ready. I'd worry more for farmers like Ted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd run a session for the discussion group. Why help your competitors?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they're not really competitors, they're my customers. If they understand robots, they'll hire me to run their robots rather than selling up to a big company. A neighbour who stays is worth more to me than a neighbour who sells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ama and Kofi in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ama, who's thirteen, to keep going with the science she loves. Kofi is ten and wants to farm, so I'd tell him to learn how the robots work, not just how to drive them. They'd both get a go on the robot tractor, of course.

I'd run a session on **robot tractors** for the discussion group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who isn't ready by 2039 wasn't paying attention. I'd say it a bit more kindly than that in public. But that's what I'd think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is great for me. I'd be 56 when the robots are good, Kwame will have moved into the drone and data side, and the kids will be grown. I'd plan to own more land and run it all with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep growing the contracting business for now and buy 80 more hectares when the Hall farm comes up for sale. I'd bring in robots gradually from about 2034, as they're proven. And I'd help Kwame move into the farm data work slowly, so it's not a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It feels like a long runway to something I can plan for. I'm quite looking forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years gives you time. What could still go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big agricultural companies could buy up the land before I can. If land prices rise because robots make farming cheaper, I might get priced out of the Hall farm. That's the one thing I'd watch closely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything for the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd encourage Kofi if he still wants to farm in five years, because he'd inherit a robot farm. Ama would go to university for science. With ten years, we can plan both without rushing.

I'd say it **kindly** in public, though privately I'd be blunter.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the contracting business and Kwame's job would both get hit before we'd fully switched. What would help is cheap loans for farmers to buy robots, so it isn't only the big companies that can afford them. And retraining for people like Kwame that's paid, not just evening classes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about land prices. If robots make farming cheaper, land prices go up and small farmers get squeezed out. Nobody's talking about that.

headlineQuote: If robots make farming cheaper, land prices go up and small farmers get squeezed out.
portrait: Priya, 43, owns an **arable and beef** farm and runs a contracting business for twelve neighbours.
She uses AI **every day** and sees robots as her next step.
Her household's risk is her husband's **software testing** job.
She is **anxious** in Steady Disruption and AGI by 2028, and **calm** with a decade.
Her long-term plan is to **buy more land** and run it with robots.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as both contracting and Kwame's job would be hit too soon.
